title: [Bad Decryption] Finally I Decrypted Cosmic Duality!
body:
Hello everyone,

After many days of intensive work trying to solve the GSMG puzzle, I've decided to share my progress publicly. While I wasn't able to find the final solution myself, I've successfully decrypted the Cosmic Duality phase and made significant breakthroughs that could help the community move forward.

I'm releasing this because I believe in collaborative problem-solving - sometimes fresh eyes can spot what we've missed. My solution includes the complete decryption process, for the final steps.

If this work proves helpful to you or contributes to solving the puzzle, please consider supporting this effort. Every contribution, no matter how small, helps sustain this kind of open research.

https://github.com/jackdevs66/GSMG5_CDuality

title: Phase 3 password is truncated in the walkthrough
body:
I hit a wall following the phase 2.2 section and it turned out to be the password, not me. The diff is
just that one line. Two hint notes at the end that you're welcome to fold in or ignore, I didn't want
to touch more of the walkthrough than needed.

## Phase 3 password

Phase 2.2 gives the assembled password as ending in `B5KR`. That does not decrypt phase 3. The FEN
goes in whole, not just the first field:

    causalitySafenetLunaHSM111100x736B6E616220726F662074756F6C69616220646E6F63657320666F206B6E697262206E6F20726F6C6C65636E61684320393030322F6E614A2F33302073656D695420656854B5KR/1r5B/2R5/2b1p1p1/2P1k1P1/1p2P2p/1P2P2P/3N1N2 b - - 0 1

Slashes, spaces and the trailing `b - - 0 1` included. sha256 of that is

    1a57c572caf3cf722e41f5f9cf99ffacff06728a43032dd44c481c77d2ec30d5

and phase 3 then decrypts to the text starting "What if the merovingian is wrong."

The encryption takes that digest as the passphrase rather than the password itself, same as phase 2,
so:

    openssl enc -d -aes-256-cbc -a -md sha256 \
      -pass pass:1a57c572caf3cf722e41f5f9cf99ffacff06728a43032dd44c481c77d2ec30d5 \
      -in phase3.txt

Line 108 above it already has the full FEN, so it looks like it just got clipped when the parts were
assembled on line 109. Following the README as written you get garbage with no clue why.

## 2021-03-01, "fefefe is 101 010"

The README lists this one as unsolved. It is the hex digits read as odd or even. F is 15, odd, so 1.
E is 14, even, so 0. FEFEFE gives 101010, which is 42.

Same rule on the other two colours: `#FFF200` gives 111000, `#3F48CC` gives 110000.

## 2020-01-14, "Yellow has a number and so does Blue"

The numbers look like 9 and 15, and they match something already known.

Sampling puzzle.png on the 14x14 grid I get 9 yellow cells and 15 blue. Taking the counter-clockwise
spiral used in phase 0 and numbering from 0, all 24 of those cells land on indices congruent to
7 mod 8, which is the last bit of each byte. Reading blue as 1 and yellow as 0 along those 24
positions:

    111101110011110110010010

and the low bit of each character of `gsmg.io/theseedisplanted`:

    111101110011110110010010

Same string, and the 15 blue cells line up with the 15 one bits, the 9 yellow with the 9 zero bits.

So the counts match the URL's low bits under this reading. I don't think they give a new input to
`yellowblueprimes`, though obviously that only rules out this interpretation. Noting it in case it
saves someone repeating it.

The two hint sections are just notes, no diff for them. Say the word if you want them written into
the timeline and I'll send a second PR.

title: Looking for primary 2019-2020 captures, raw chat history, and any clear answer on derivability
body:
Moving these out of #10 so they don't get lost when it merges, as asked.

Revised down from what I first wrote in the PR thread. Two of the three I've since answered myself, so I'm only leaving what's actually still open.

**Withdrawn: raw Telegram history.** I found it. `halbgott29a/gsmgio-5btc-puzzle` has a 181k line `_work/chat_transcript.txt`. Anyone else stuck on the screenshots should start there rather than asking.

**Narrowed: local captures of gsmg.io.** The site is still live and still serving the original chain, so this is not the broad ask I made in the PR. `/theseedisplanted`, `/choiceisanillusion...` and `/89727c59...` all return 200 with the original content today, and the images are byte identical to archived copies. What would still help is anything that existed in 2019 or 2020 and is **no longer served**. A page that was up briefly and then removed wouldn't be in the live site or necessarily in the CDX index, and that's the only gap left here.

**Still open, and the one I care about: did Jrk ever plainly say whether the final step is derivable from published material alone?**

He has said things that read both ways. "Everything is solvable" points one way. The 2026-07-12 messages point the other: "my close friends have the best chance of solving it (a few tried), but they don't have the skills some of you do. NOTE: that is a hint." That reads like the last step depends on something he knows rather than something published.

This matters because three people working independently have now reached the same conclusion from different directions, that no function of the published artifacts produces the prize key. vadiksh85-pixel set it out in puzzlehunt/gsmgio-5btc-puzzle#82 and also made the structural point: `1GSMG1...` is a vanity address, so its key was brute forced and is random with respect to every artifact in the puzzle. A random key can't be the output of a derivation over those artifacts. I've reproduced that poster's committed matrix invariants exactly against my own decrypt (S=5193, Wr=268603, Wc=268828), so their data is sound.

If Jrk confirmed either way somewhere, a pointer to it would settle whether the remaining work is a cipher problem or a delivery problem. #82 asked essentially this and got no answer.

title: Add two Phase 0 observations to the unverified section
body:
Follow-up to #10, which you asked me to keep as a one-line fix. These are the two hint notes from that PR description, written into the timeline so they aren't buried once #10 merges.

Both go where the README already discusses the relevant hint. No other changes.

**2020-01-14, "Yellow has a number and so does Blue."** The section currently ends "no one publicly managed to decode it". The two numbers look like 9 and 15, and they turn out to restate the URL's low bits rather than supply anything new: the 24 coloured cells all sit at spiral indices 7 mod 8, and reading blue as 1 and yellow as 0 reproduces the low bit of each character of `gsmg.io/theseedisplanted` exactly. So it rules that reading out as an input to `yellowblueprimes`. Worth having written down so nobody redoes it.

**2021-03-01, "fefefe is 101 010."** This is hex digit parity: F is 15, odd, so 1; E is 14, even, so 0, giving `101010` = 42. I've attributed it as a solver's remark rather than an official hint, since the message is from Janusz Baran and not Jrk, and I've noted that the `104` half of the same message doesn't agree with the cell's spiral index. Correcting my own framing in #10, which implied it was a listed hint.

Happy to reword either note if you'd rather they read differently.

title: Proposed first step toward solving the DBBI and FAED blocks and obtaining a block beginning with BTCSEED
body: This is a possible lead concerning the two still-unsolved SalPhaseIon blocks, usually referred to as DBBI and FAED after their first few letters. Using a Bifid cipher, this method produces a new 570-character block beginning with: ```text BTCSEED ``` I do not consider this a confirmed solution to SalPhaseIon. At this stage, it is simply a reproducible path that gives an interesting enough result to be included in the Unverified section. ## 1. The two starting blocks ### DBBI block ```text d b b i b f b h c c b e g b i h a b e b e i h b e g g e g e b e b b g e h h e b h h f b a b f d h b e f f c d b b f c c c g b f b e e g g e c b e d c i b f b f f g i g b e e e a b e ``` Without spaces: ```text dbbibfbhccbegbihabebeihbeggegebebbgehhebhhfbabfdhbeffcdbbfcccgbfbeeggecbedcibfbffgigbeeeabe ``` This block contains 91 characters. ### FAED block ```text f a e d g g e e d f c b d a b h h g g c a d c f e d d g f d g b g i g a a e d g g i a f a e c g h g g c d a i h e h a h b a h i g c e i f g b f g e f g a i f a b i f a g a e g e a c g b b e a g f g g e e g g a f b a c g f c d b e i f f a a f c i d a h g d e e f g h h c g g a e g d e b h h e g e g h c e g a d f b d i a g e f c i c g g i f d c g a a g g f b i g a i c f b h e c a e c b c e i a i c e b g b g i e c d e g g f g e g a e d g g f i i c i i i f i f h g g c g f g d c d g g e f c b e e i g e f i b g i b g g g h h f b c g i f d e h e d f d a g i c d b h i c g a i e d a e h a h g h h c i h d g h f h b i i c e c b i i c h i h i i i g i d d g e h h d f d c h c b a f g f b h a h e a g e g e c a f e h g c f g g g g c a g f h h g h b a i h i d i e h h f d e g g d g c i h g g g g g h a d a h i g i g b g e c g e d f c d g g a c c d e h i i c i g f b f f h g g a e i d b b e i b b e i i f d g f d h i e e e i e e e c i f d g d a h d i g g f h e g f i a f f i g g b c b c e h c e a b f b e d b i i b f b f d e d e e h g i g f a a i g g a g b e i i c h i e d i f b e h g b c c a h h b i i b i b b i b d c b a h a i d h f a h i i h i c ``` Without spaces: ```text  ``` This second block contains exactly 570 characters. ## 2. Building the alphabet from DBBI The idea is simply to take the DBBI block and remove letters that have already appeared, while keeping the order of their first occurrence. The beginning gives: ```text d b b i b f b h c c b e g b i h a ``` Keeping each letter only once gives: ```text d b i f h c e g a ``` This gives: ```text DBIFHCEGA ``` It is actually not necessary to use all 91 characters to obtain this sequence, since all the useful letters appear very early in the block. Using the entire block gives the same result. The remaining unused letters of the alphabet are then added in alphabetical order, with J removed as in a standard Bifid square. This gives: ```text DBIFHCEGAKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ ``` The corresponding 5×5 grid is: ```text D B I F H C E G A K L M N O P Q R S T U V W X Y Z ``` ## 3. Decrypting FAED with this grid The complete FAED block is used as the ciphertext: ```text  ``` In the dCode Bifid decoder, the following settings are used: ```text Alphabet: DBIFHCEGAKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ Grid: D B I F H C E G A K L M N O P Q R S T U V W X Y Z Period / Blocks Length: 570 Coordinates Reading Mode: Row-Column (Normal mode) ``` The value 570 simply comes from the length of the complete FAED block. ## 4. Result With these settings, the complete 570-character result is: ```text  ``` The first seven characters immediately give: ```text BTCSEED ``` There is also another interesting detail in the result: the letter z appears only once in the entire 570-character output. If we separate the result around this single z, while also isolating BTCSEED, it becomes much easier to see: ```text BTCSEED deoemckeadhbschdkbdcsdkdvbxcpcochcrdicibqeebddbcndsbdcpdgcpdncncsescgddclenbmcuducqcacdeld z  ``` The structure is therefore: ```text BTCSEED + 90 characters + z + 472 characters ``` The z is character number 98 in the complete 570-character result. The result can be reproduced in dCode as shown in the screenshot below: ## 5. Why I think this lead is worth keeping What I find interesting here is not only the appearance of BTCSEED, but also the small number of steps needed to obtain it. We start from the two blocks we are already trying to understand: ```text DBBI FAED ``` The first one naturally gives an alphabet after removing repeated letters: ```text DBBI ↓ DBIFHCEGA ↓ DBIFHCEGAKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ ``` This alphabet can then be used directly as a Bifid grid. FAED is used as-is, with its full length of 570 as the period, and the result immediately begins with: ```text BTCSEED ``` There is no need to test hundreds of different keys or periods to obtain this particular result. That is why I think this path is worth documenting, even though the whole output is not yet understood. ## 6. The single z and its similarity with SalPhaseIon The single z in the Bifid result may also be worth paying attention to because SalPhaseIon already uses z as a separator. In the original SalPhaseIon material, z characters separate some of the different encoded sections. The structure seen there is essentially of the form: ```text ... z ... z ... ``` Some of these separated sections were later decoded into values such as: ```text lastwordsbeforearchichoice thispassword ``` So z already has an identifiable structural role elsewhere in SalPhaseIon. This makes the fact that the Bifid output contains exactly one z interesting. The output can therefore provisionally be viewed as: ```text BTCSEED deoemckeadhbschdkbdcsdkdvbxcpcochcrdicibqeebddbcndsbdcpdgcpdncncsescgddclenbmcuducqcacdeld Z  ``` I am not claiming that this z definitely has the same function here. But the similarity is worth recording: * SalPhaseIon already uses z as a separator. * The 570-character Bifid result contains exactly one z. * The z appears after BTCSEED and another 90 characters. * It divides the remaining output into two clearly defined parts. This gives us another structural feature to investigate instead of looking only at the appearance of BTCSEED. ## 7. What remains to be understood The main problem is still that the characters after BTCSEED do not immediately produce readable English. Before the z we have: ```text deoemckeadhbschdkbdcsdkdvbxcpcochcrdicibqeebddbcndsbdcpdgcpdncncsescgddclenbmcuducqcacdeld ``` Then: ```text z ``` And after the z: ```text  ``` There are also many recurring structures involving b, c, d and e. In some places these letters appear at the end of groups, while elsewhere similar-looking structures seem to appear in reverse, with these letters at the beginning. This part is not solved yet, but it may suggest that what follows BTCSEED is not random noise and could contain another transformation or encoding layer. ## Current state For now, I would summarize the proposed path like this: ```text DBBI ↓ remove repeated letters ↓ DBIFHCEGA ↓ complete the Bifid alphabet ↓ DBIFHCEGAKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ ↓ Bifid decryption of FAED Period = 570 Row-Column ↓ BTCSEED ↓ 90 characters ↓ Z ↓ 472 characters still to understand ``` BTCSEED is reproducible with this method. The presence of a single z is also interesting because z already acts as a separator elsewhere in SalPhaseIon. The open question is whether the material on either side of this z contains another layer of encryption, encoding or transformation. At this stage, this is only a proposed path. I do not know whether this is the route JRK intended us to find, or whether the appearance of BTCSEED and the position of the z are intentional.

title: Chain-2 (inner blob) independently re-verified end to end; WIF-chain pattern breaks at the cosmic blob; where should its password come from?
body:
## 1. Independent re-verification of chain 2

The trailing blob on the phase-3.2 page (salt `b45a5e3d`) decrypts with `WIF(K_C1)` (EVP-MD5, AES-256-CBC) into a clean 79-byte payload:

```
K_S1 = b06fa6f20561756c865dac7190f063480a371e4a13206e529ee7e9078f309c4b
K_S2 = b11d211ca0a17cd68c580308f3e6f21d3f935c8da3c4373b6f73ab5ccfaea597
E_S  = 740a25de4b8e946d0a5ae2667a23a2
```

`E_S` matches the documented value exactly, and the PKCS7 padding is valid, so this link (chain1 -> WIF(K_C1) -> chain2) is solid, not a false positive.

## 2. The natural continuation fails on the cosmic blob

If each blob's password were WIF(K1 of the previous payload), the cosmic blob (salt `2d3f6fe0`) should open with `WIF(K_S1)`. It does not. I tested:

- WIF(K_S1), WIF(K_S2), compressed WIFs of both, uppercase/lowercase
- WIF(K_C2) (the other chain1 key), compressed and uncompressed
- raw/hex of K_S1/K_S2/E_C/E_S, `E_C||E_S`, sha256 variants
- EVP-MD5, EVP-SHA1, EVP-SHA256 and PBKDF2, AES-CBC and AES-CFB

All fail (no valid padding, no readable output). So either the chain pattern changes at the cosmic blob (the way the unverified fork's chain4 password `E_C||E_S||E_B[:2]` departs from the WIF pattern), or the cosmic blob's password comes from somewhere else entirely.

## 3. New candidates, computed for the first time as far as I can tell

In case anyone wants to sweep them against other artifacts:

```
WIF(K_S1) = 5K9zQVotw2zgW4FpnfwyFLSe4Zk3FGrqypC4JFvE4oN62PnTxB6
WIF(K_S2) = 5KAHiT77VJYuHRQF7PuApvxnfkyrNVcd5v4BHKTabvuZf7Y9BPv
WIF(K_C2) = 5HyaKEytxN9PhhQvPYfsyNwzzK6Hfsx6DxyUBa3CfcHWizdj8LD
WIFc(K_S1) = L38gNi9zDVobMFNRvaudGGpAajWxv111BmHoZAqvfme5B5K5WFcF
WIFc(K_S2) = L39zmxDydvTomUhbHE5GNZBEa57vusJEGhB2P2UKKAw197hejJWv
```

None of them opens the cosmic blob, the two phase-2 blobs, or reproduces the prize address as a scalar.

## 4. The actual question

@Naddiseo you have said that a true cosmic decryption should be "plain text readable English". Two questions:

1. Is that expectation something the creator communicated to you directly (or that you saw in material not in the repo), or is it an inference from how every other blob in the puzzle behaves?
2. Is there any indication anywhere of where the cosmic blob's password is supposed to come from? The creator's 2023-02-23 message lists `yellow blue primes matrixsumlist lastwordsbeforearchichoice yinyang` and says the password is "in front of your eyes". I've tested that ingredient list in the phase-3 style (sha256 of concatenated resolutions, all orderings and many value assignments, ~2,400 candidates) and lexically, plus sha256 readings of the remaining board tokens (`shabef anstoo` = sha256 + operand, etc.), with no hit.

For context on the two undecoded streams (DBBI 91, FAED 570): the digit stream contains no zero at all (which for the z-section trick, hex->decimal, would force a plaintext with no p/P/spaces/0), the letter arrangement passes uniform-random tests on pairs/triplets, and saama143's a/b/c expansion to 13x13 and 35x35 reads as noise under row/column/serpentine/spiral orderings with base-3 interpretations. So if there is something known about the *kind* of thing those two blocks are (checksum, filler, key material rather than text), that would narrow the search space a lot.
